4.text: other hand, when in 1895, during a brawl at the Anui fair, a Reindeer Chukchee

10.text: A considerable part of their former intractability remains at the present

22.text: The Chukchee, when angry, growls, shows his teeth, and makes a threatening

23.text: bite on his sleeve or on the handle of his knife, in defiance of his foe. Some

24.text: of them, when angered, shed tears of rage, and tear their hair like unruly children.

25.text: Their language is singularly poor in abusive terms, and quarrels are

31.text: 1896 on the Poplar River, an affluent of the Small Anui, a young man killed

32.text: his brother in order to get possession of his flock. The murderer, with his

33.text: accomplice and their victim, arranged a contest of jumping over a barrier,

34.text: the loser to pay the forfeit of skipping about for a while with his feet and

35.text: hands bound together. When the elder brother lost, the other two men

36.text: accordingly tied his feet, and coolly stabbed him with their knives. I heard

37.text: the details of both deeds from the murderers themselves.

38.text: In the tale of “Elendi and his Sons,” published in my “Chukchee Materials,”

39.text: Elendi, to avenge the treachery of his slave, kills him in a most cruel manner.

40.text: With sharp stakes he fastens the slave’s hands, feet, the fleshy parts of his

41.text: sides, and the skin of his scalp, to the ground, and then makes both of his

42.text: wives urinate and defecate into his mouth.¹
